conditions.unmeasured: figures downstream of a constant nobody has measured are absent rather than estimated
conditions.what_an_interval_here_is: a statement about this model's declared inputs, and nothing about whether the model has the right structure (ch14, ch19)

produced_by.sampler: sizing.mc — inverse transform, Iman-Conover rank correlation

correlations.because: Both are quoted by the same supply chain in the same quarter. A year when drives are scarce is usually a year when servers are, and treating them as independent narrows the interval on capital cost by pretending one can save you from the other.

More data stored is usually more data read. This one changes the answer rather than just the interval: the two chains that compete inside nodes_total are driven by these two inputs, so correlating them changes how often each constraint binds.

summary.description: The storage model as it stands at the end of the_five_year_model, built by bench/stages.py from models/storage_cluster/model.yaml. Not a model anybody would ship: it is the finished model with everything the book has not introduced yet removed, so that a reader can see what it looked like when it had 50 nodes in it.

provenance.source: ch04 — lognormal because growth compounds and cannot be negative. The p10/p90 say: surprised below 12% a year, surprised above 60%.

average_usable_capacity.label: average usable capacity
average_usable_capacity.note: The mean of the day-one and horizon capacities: a straight line drawn under a curve that is not straight, which understates the area. Stated rather than hidden, because a unit cost is only as defensible as its denominator (ch17).

provenance.source: ch11 — rebuild reserve plus allocator behaviour near full. One node's worth of data has to land somewhere when a node dies, and a filesystem at 97% is a different filesystem.

chassis, CPU, memory and boot media, less drives. Lognormal like any price, and wider than the drives' because a chassis is a configuration rather than a commodity — which is why ch19 finds it at the top of the tornado

cost_per_usable_tb_month.label: cost per usable TB per month
cost_per_usable_tb_month.note: The formula divides by a horizon in years and the node is declared in months. Those two have identical dimensions and differ by a factor of twelve, so a check that compared only dimensions would publish a figure twelve times too large and pass. sizing/units.py converts.

provenance.source: datasheet capacity. Decimal TB, not TiB — appendix D, and it is a 10% difference

street price per decimal TB at this capacity point, three quotes. Lognormal because prices move by ratios rather than by amounts, and because three quotes give a centre and a spread rather than a shape
chassis choice
all-in delivered rate including transmission. Lognormal: it cannot go negative and its history is multiplicative

facility_power.label: facility power
facility_power.note: watts in, kilowatts out — the build converts, nobody divides by a thousand by hand

ceiling.because: A cluster that is full cannot rebuild a failed node, and one that is nearly full allocates badly long before that. The margin is the same node the sizing used, so the two cannot drift apart (ch11). Over the limit means out of space; inside the headroom means the rebuild reserve has been spent on data.

provenance.source: salary, employer costs, tooling and overhead. Lognormal because pay is right-skewed and cannot go negative; the p90 is a senior engineer in an expensive city
the refresh cycle this cluster is bought against
by definition, 365.25 x 24. The quarter-day is worth about a fifth of a per cent over five years — less than this model's other errors, and free to get right

filesystem, index and journal overhead as a multiplier on stored bytes. Triangular, and the bounds are for objects of the size this model assumes — the real spread is a function of object size, which is a term ch09 says this model lacks

switch ports, optics and cabling, amortised per node. Triangular rather than lognormal, although it is a price: it is a bill of materials divided by a node count somebody chose, so the bounds are the plausible designs rather than a market

typical draw under load, per chassis as configured. Triangular, and one of the few inputs here whose bounds are physical rather than editorial: a chassis cannot draw less than it idles at, or more than its supply will give it
sustained sequential read per node, as quoted. Unverified here — ch03. Triangular, and the lower bound is the one doing the work: the quoted figure is sequential and a real read pattern is not

nodes_purchased.label: nodes purchased
nodes_purchased.note:
**The most important node in this model, and the one a spreadsheet hides.** Sizing does not produce a cluster; it produces a recommendation, and then a person decides. That decision is made once, before the five years happen, and everything downstream of it — every dollar of capital, every watt, every ceiling — is a consequence of the number chosen here and not of the number the model would recommend in hindsight.
Deriving it instead would make the ceilings below tautologies: a cluster sized to satisfy a fill limit satisfies it in every sample, and the model would cheerfully report a zero per cent chance of running out of space. Making it an input is what lets the ceilings ask the only question worth asking — *given what we actually bought, how often does the world break it?*

provenance.source: the sizing decision, taken the way it is usually taken: nodes_recommended evaluated at every input's point estimate. That is exactly 121, and the ceilings below are what the same model says about that decision once the inputs are allowed to be uncertain. Change this number and watch them move — that is the exercise of ch12

nodes_recommended.label: nodes the model recommends
nodes_recommended.note: The first place a reader meets a binding constraint. Two independent chains produce two node counts and you buy the larger, which means that across this model's uncertainty the answer is sometimes set by capacity and sometimes by bandwidth — and an average of the two is a cluster that satisfies neither.

measured.corpus: bench.measure.mixed_objects — synthetic mixture of text, columnar, already-compressed and sparse objects, seeds 0-7

one_year.label: one year
one_year.note: Here because a duration cannot be an exponent. In (1+r)^n the n is a pure number, so the horizon has to be divided by something with the same units before it can be used as one. Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.

provenance.source: definition
ch03 — the busy hour, not the average. Triangular because this is an engineer's min/likely/max and pretending to more shape than that would be invention.

ch15 — facility overhead. A multiplier on IT load, and the single number a colocation contract is most likely to disagree with you about. Triangular: the minimum is a good building, the maximum is a poor one, and below one is impossible

ceiling.because: Not a hard limit but a queueing one (ch06). Response time climbs long before a device is saturated, so the margin here is about latency rather than capacity — which is why it is a different number from capacity_headroom and declared separately rather than shared.

provenance.source: three copies. An erasure-coded cluster substitutes its own overhead factor here and the rest of the model is unchanged, which is the point of it being a node.

fraction of one engineer this cluster occupies. Triangular, and the shape cannot express what actually happens: people are not divisible, so the real distribution is lumpy in the way ch08 calls a regime change

annual support as a fraction of capital cost. Triangular because it is negotiated inside a band the market sets rather than drawn from one: the spread is what different buyers get, not what varies from year to year
stated workload (ch02) — what the application says it needs to store today

scenario.because: The same conditions the finished model is quoted under, so that a number from a stage and a number from the whole model differ only by what the stage does not contain yet.
